pl-l4d14c2-d1e112.summary: Says penance is named from punishing, by which one punishes the unlawful things one did; the virtue of penance is conceived by fear.
claims: Penance is named from punishing.
Penance is conceived by fear.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e118.summary: Cites Isaiah: from your fear, Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation.
claims: Fear conceives salvation.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e121.summary: Gives Ambrose's definition: penance is to lament past evils and not commit again what must be lamented.
claims: Penance is lamenting past evils and not repeating them.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e130.summary: Gives Gregory: to repent is to weep for past sins and not commit what must be wept for; whoever laments some sins while committing others either does not know how to repent or pretends; what profit is there in weeping for lust while still panting with avarice?
claims: Repenting of some sins while committing others is not true penance.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e140.summary: Reports some who, clinging too strongly to these words, contend that one who truly repents never again sins damnably, and that if he sins gravely, true penance did not precede.
claims: Some hold that true penance excludes later mortal sin.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e143.summary: Notes they support this with other testimonies.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e146.summary: Quotes Isidore: one who still does what he repents of is a mocker, not a penitent, like a dog returning to its vomit; many weep constantly and do not stop sinning; one is washed and clean who laments past sins and does not repeat them, washed but not clean who laments and repeats.
claims: One who repeats his sins is a mocker, not a penitent.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e152.summary: Quotes Augustine: penance stained by subsequent fault is vain; laments profit nothing if sins are repeated; it is worthless to ask pardon for evils and then repeat them.
claims: Penance followed by relapse is vain.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e161.summary: Quotes Gregory: whoever laments his deeds but does not abandon them subjects himself to graver punishment.
claims: Lamenting without abandoning sin increases punishment.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e170.summary: Quotes Ambrose: some think penance can be done often, who are wanton in Christ; if they truly repented, they would not think it to be repeated, since as there is one baptism, so there is one penance.
claims: Ambrose: as there is one baptism, there is one penance.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e180.summary: Notes that they use these and other texts to assert their opinion.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e183.summary: Cites Ambrose: true penance is to cease from sin.
claims: True penance is ceasing from sin.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e192.summary: Adds Ambrose: it is great progress to have renounced error; to strip and amend minds steeped in vice belongs to perfect virtue and heavenly grace.
claims: Renouncing vice is the work of heavenly grace.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e201.summary: Defines penance soundly: the virtue or grace by which we lament and hate the evils we have committed, with a purpose of amendment, and do not will to commit again what must be lamented; true penance is to grieve and hate vices in the soul.
claims: Penance is the virtue by which we lament and hate past evils with purpose of amendment.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e204.summary: Interprets 'to repent is to weep for past deeds and not commit what is to be wept for' as referring not to different times but to the same time: while one weeps for evils done, one does not commit, in will or deed, things to be wept for; as the following words suggest.
claims: The definition concerns the same time, not the whole future.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e213.summary: Quotes Augustine: no one should think that the crimes that exclude from God's kingdom may be committed daily and redeemed daily by alms; life must be changed for the better, and God propitiated by alms for past sins, not bought so that one may sin with impunity; he gives no one license to sin, though he mercifully blots out sins if fitting satisfaction is not neglected.
claims: Alms do not purchase license to sin.
Life must be changed, and satisfaction made.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e223.summary: Quotes Pope Pius: fasting, prayer, and other religious works profit nothing unless the mind is turned from iniquity.
claims: Good works profit only if the mind turns from sin.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e229.summary: Concludes that whoever so recalls his mind from evils that he laments what he did, does not will to commit what must be lamented, and does not neglect satisfaction, truly repents; it is not untrue penance because later he sins, not by intent but by chance or weakness. The mocker is one who laments while not ceasing to sin in will or deed; one who repeats what he wept for is washed for a time, but that cleanness is not sufficient for salvation, being momentary, not persevering.
claims: True penance includes lament, will not to sin, and satisfaction.
Later sin from weakness does not falsify earlier penance.
Momentary cleanness does not suffice for salvation.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e241.summary: Interprets 'penance stained by later fault is vain': it lacks the fruit of penance not followed by sin, which is escape from hell and attainment of glory. Later sin kills that penance and earlier good works, so they do not receive their reward; but if the later sin is repented, the earlier penance and good works revive, those done in charity, which alone are living; works done without charity are born dead and cannot revive.
claims: Later sin kills earlier merits.
Penance revives merits done in charity.
Works done without charity cannot revive.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e248.summary: Interprets 'laments profit nothing' similarly: if sins are repeated, earlier lament does not avail for salvation or final pardon, since nothing remains of purity of life: either forgiven sins return, as some hold, or, if not, the person is made as guilty through ingratitude as if they had returned. Whether sins return will be treated more fully later.
claims: Relapse leaves one as guilty as if forgiven sins returned.
Whether forgiven sins return is deferred.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e257.summary: Interprets 'it is worthless to ask pardon and repeat evils' similarly, as worthless for salvation or purity of life.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e260.summary: Applies this to Augustine's saying: penance is a vengeance of one grieving, punishing in himself what he grieves to have done.
claims: Penance is self-punishment for sin.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e269.summary: Quotes Augustine further: one must grieve continually for sin, as 'poenitere' means 'poenam tenere', always punishing in oneself what one committed. Where grief ends, penance ends; if penance ends, what remains of pardon? Let him hope in grace as long as penance sustains him; 'go and sin no more' means let not even the will to sin arise, which is kept only by continual grief. Let him always grieve and rejoice in grief, from faith.
claims: Penance is continual grief for sin.
Where penance ends, pardon is lost.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e278.summary: Interprets that 'penance is vengeance always punishing what one did' concerns the penance of the perfect, or penance sufficient for salvation.
claims: Continual penance describes the penance of the perfect.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e284.summary: States that 'if penance ends, nothing of pardon remains' can be taken in two ways.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e291.summary: First reading: if, as some think, forgiven sins return, it is easy to see that nothing of pardon remains, since they are repeated; as a freed slave is truly free yet recalled to servitude for an offense, so the penitent's sins are truly forgiven yet return because of a repeated offense.
claims: On one view forgiven sins return upon relapse.

pl-l4d14c2-d1e294.summary: Second reading: if they do not return, nothing of pardon remains not because forgiven sins are imputed again, but because through ingratitude one becomes as guilty and unclean as if they had returned.
claims: On the other view, ingratitude makes one as guilty as if sins returned.

pl-l4d14c2.summary: Penance is named from punishing, punishing one's unlawful deeds, and is conceived by fear. Ambrose and Gregory define it as lamenting past sins and not committing again what must be lamented. Some take this strictly, holding that one who truly repents never again sins mortally, and that later grave sin shows prior penance was not true, citing Isidore, Augustine, Gregory, and Ambrose ('as there is one baptism, so one penance'). Lombard defines penance as the virtue or grace by which we lament and hate the evils done with purpose of amendment and will not commit them again; the 'not committing' refers to the same time as the weeping. True penance is not voided by later sin through weakness; 'penance stained by later sin is vain' means it loses its fruit, though good works done in charity revive when the later sin is repented. Augustine's 'penance as continual vengeance' concerns the penance of the perfect. 'If penance ends, nothing of pardon remains' holds whether forgiven sins return or not, since ingratitude makes one as guilty.
claims: Penance is named from punishing and is conceived by fear.
Penance is lamenting past sins and not committing them again.
Lombard defines penance as the virtue by which we lament and hate past evils with purpose of amendment.
Later sin through weakness does not show that earlier penance was false.
Works done in charity, killed by later sin, revive through penance.
Ingratitude by relapse makes one as guilty as if forgiven sins returned.
